cases.question: Which units are vacant right now?

usage.review_restated: For every unit that has no lease whose status is flagged as current, the query lists the building, city, unit number, type, bedrooms, square footage, the rent recorded on the unit, and the latest end date across all of that unit's leases. It returns 50 rows, sorted by building name and unit number.

cases.title: Units vacant right now (no lease currently in effect)
cases.sql:
SELECT b.name AS building,
       b.city AS city,
       u.unit_number AS unit_number,
       u.unit_type AS unit_type,
       u.bedrooms AS bedrooms,
       u.sqft AS sqft,
       u.monthly_rent AS asking_rent,
       (SELECT MAX(l3.end_date) FROM lease l3 WHERE l3.unit_id = u.unit_id) AS last_lease_end_date
FROM unit u
JOIN building b ON b.building_id = u.building_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM lease l
        JOIN lease_status ls ON ls.status_id = l.status_id
        WHERE l.unit_id = u.unit_id
          AND ls.is_current = 1
      )
ORDER BY b.name, u.unit_number
assumptions: A unit is vacant when it has no lease in a status that is flagged as current — i.e. no Active - Fixed Term, Active - Month to Month or Notice Given lease. Notice Given still counts as occupied, because the tenant is still living there until the notice period ends.

Leases marked Ended, Evicted or Pending Signature do not occupy a unit, even where their stored dates still span today (e.g. a tenant who left early, was evicted, or never signed). 24 units fall in exactly this situation.
The asking rent shown is the rent recorded on the unit, not the rent of any past lease.
'Last lease end date' is the latest end date recorded on any lease for the unit; it is blank for units whose only lease is still open-ended.
Unit numbers repeat across buildings, so each row is identified by building plus unit number.

cases.question: List tenants who currently have a lease, with their unit and monthly rent.

usage.review_restated: The SQL returns one row for each lease whose status is flagged as current, showing the tenant's name and contact details, the building and unit, the unit's type and bedrooms, the unit's recorded rent, the lease status and the lease start date, sorted by building, unit and tenant name.

cases.title: Tenants with a current lease, their unit and monthly rent
cases.sql:
SELECT
  t.first_name || ' ' || t.last_name AS tenant_name,
  t.email AS tenant_email,
  t.phone AS tenant_phone,
  b.name AS building,
  u.unit_number AS unit,
  u.unit_type AS unit_type,
  u.bedrooms AS bedrooms,
  u.monthly_rent AS monthly_rent,
  ls.label AS lease_status,
  l.start_date AS lease_start_date
FROM lease l
JOIN lease_status ls ON ls.status_id = l.status_id
JOIN tenant t ON t.tenant_id = l.tenant_id
JOIN unit u ON u.unit_id = l.unit_id
JOIN building b ON b.building_id = u.building_id
WHERE ls.is_current = 1
ORDER BY b.name, u.unit_number, tenant_name
assumptions: "Currently have a lease" = the lease is in force today: its status is flagged as current in the system, which covers Active - Fixed Term, Active - Month to Month, and Notice Given (tenants who have given notice but are still under lease). Pending Signature, Ended and Evicted leases are excluded.
Monthly rent is the rent recorded for the unit the lease covers.
Each tenant appears once, with the unit on their current lease.
The lease status is shown so you can tell fixed-term, month-to-month and notice-given tenants apart.

Check: The query lists one row per current lease, not one per tenant, and nothing removes repeats, so a tenant with two current leases would appear twice even though the assumptions say each tenant appears once. Check whether any tenant name repeats in the 109 rows before sharing.

cases.question: How many maintenance requests are still open in each building?

usage.review_restated: For each of the 12 buildings, the SQL counts maintenance requests whose state is exactly 'open', attributing each request to the building that holds its unit, and lists the building name, street and city with that count, sorted highest count first. Buildings with no matching requests show 0.

cases.title: Open maintenance requests by building
cases.sql:
SELECT b.name AS building,
       b.street AS street,
       b.city AS city,
       COUNT(m.request_id) AS open_requests
FROM building b
LEFT JOIN unit u ON u.building_id = b.building_id
LEFT JOIN maintenance m ON m.unit_id = u.unit_id AND m.state = 'open'
GROUP BY b.building_id, b.name, b.street, b.city
ORDER BY open_requests DESC, b.name
assumptions: "Still open" means requests whose status is currently Open (27 in total); requests that are In progress or Waiting for parts are not counted.
Each request is counted once, attributed to the building that contains its unit.
All 12 buildings are listed, including those with no open requests (shown as 0).
No date range was applied – all requests regardless of when they were opened.

Check: The SQL counts only requests in the exact 'open' state, so In progress and Waiting for parts requests are left out. If "still open" means not yet closed, as is common in maintenance reporting, the per-building counts undercount; confirm with the requester which meaning they intend before sharing.

cases.question: Which tenants paid rent late at least once in 2026?

usage.review_restated: For each tenant with at least one rent payment whose due date falls in 2026 and whose payment date is after that due date, the query returns the tenant's name and email, the count of such late payments, the earliest and latest late due dates, the largest number of days paid after due, and the total

cases.title: Tenants who paid rent late at least once in 2026
cases.sql: SELECT t.first_name || ' ' || t.last_name AS tenant, t.email AS tenant_email, COUNT(*) AS late_payments, MIN(p.due_on) AS first_late_rent_due, MAX(p.due_on) AS most_recent_late_rent_due, MAX(CAST(julianday(p.paid_on) - julianday(p.due_on) AS INTEGER)) AS worst_days_late, ROUND(SUM(p.amount), 2) AS total_paid_late FROM payment p JOIN lease l ON p.lease_id = l.lease_id JOIN tenant t ON l.tenant_id = t.tenant_id WHERE p.due_on >= '2026-01-01' AND p.due_on < '2027-01-01' AND p.paid_on > p.due_on GROUP BY t.tenant_id, t.first_name, t.last_name, t.email ORDER BY late_payments DESC, worst_days_late DESC, tenant
assumptions: "Late" means the payment date is after the rent due date; unpaid rent is not counted as late.
"In 2026" means rent instalments due between 1 Jan and 31 Dec 2026 (payments actually received in 2026 give the same late set).
Each lease belongs to one tenant, so no risk of double counting a person.
Tenants are identified by first and last name plus email, since names repeat.

Check: The filter is on the due date, not the payment date, so a rent instalment due in late 2026 but paid in 2027 is counted as a 2026 late payment. The assumption that filtering on payment date gives the same set is not guaranteed, so check whether "paid late in 2026" should instead filter on when the payment was made.

cases.question: Total rent collected per region in 2026.

usage.review_restated: For each region, this SQL counts the payments dated 1 January 2026 through 31 December 2026 (by paid date, on payments linked through lease, unit and building to a region) and sums their amounts, rounded to two decimals, sorted from highest to lowest total.

cases.title: Rent collected by region in 2026
cases.sql:
SELECT r.name AS region,
       COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payments_received,
       ROUND(SUM(p.amount), 2) AS rent_collected
FROM payment p
JOIN lease l ON p.lease_id = l.lease_id
JOIN unit u ON l.unit_id = u.unit_id
JOIN building b ON u.building_id = b.building_id
JOIN region r ON b.region_id = r.region_id
WHERE p.paid_on >= '2026-01-01'
  AND p.paid_on < '2027-01-01'
GROUP BY r.name
ORDER BY rent_collected DESC
assumptions: "Collected" means money actually received, so I counted by the date the payment was received (in 2026) rather than by the rent period it covered.
Unpaid invoices (no received date) are excluded, since nothing was collected on them.
Rent is attributed to the region of the building the leased unit belongs to.
All payment records are treated as rent payments.
No date range default was given, so the calendar year 2026 (1 Jan – 31 Dec) is used.

cases.question: Urgent maintenance requests that are not closed, with the technician assigned.

usage.review_restated: This SQL returns one row for each maintenance request whose priority is exactly 'urgent' and whose state is not 'closed', showing its open date, status, category, building, unit number, and assigned technician's name (or 'Unassigned' when none is recorded), with the technician's active flag, ordered

cases.title: Urgent maintenance requests still open, with assigned technician
cases.sql:
SELECT m.request_id AS request_id,
       m.opened AS date_opened,
       m.state AS status,
       m.category AS category,
       b.name AS building,
       'Unit ' || u.unit_number AS unit,
       COALESCE(s.first_name || ' ' || s.last_name, 'Unassigned') AS technician,
       COALESCE(s.active, 0) AS technician_active
FROM maintenance AS m
JOIN unit AS u ON u.unit_id = m.unit_id
JOIN building AS b ON b.building_id = u.building_id
LEFT JOIN staff AS s ON s.staff_id = m.assigned_to
WHERE m.priority = 'urgent'
  AND m.state <> 'closed'
ORDER BY m.opened ASC, m.request_id
assumptions: "Urgent" means priority exactly urgent (high-priority requests are not included).
"Not closed" means any status other than closed: open, in progress or waiting for parts — 17 requests in total.
The assigned technician is looked up from the staff member recorded on the request; 3 of these requests have nobody assigned yet and are shown as Unassigned.
Each request is listed on its own line with the unit and building it belongs to, oldest first.

cases.question: Average number of days to close a plumbing request.

usage.review_restated: This SQL returns one row: the count of maintenance requests in category 'plumbing' with state 'closed' and a non-empty closed date, plus the average, fastest and slowest number of calendar days between opened and closed dates, across all dates.

cases.title: Average days to close plumbing requests
cases.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS closed_plumbing_requests,
       ROUND(AVG(julianday(m.closed) - julianday(m.opened)), 2) AS avg_days_to_close,
       ROUND(MIN(julianday(m.closed) - julianday(m.opened)), 2) AS fastest_days,
       ROUND(MAX(julianday(m.closed) - julianday(m.opened)), 2) AS slowest_days
FROM maintenance m
WHERE m.category = 'plumbing'
  AND m.state = 'closed'
  AND m.closed IS NOT NULL
  AND m.closed <> ''
assumptions: "Plumbing" means requests whose category is stored as plumbing.
Only requests already closed are measured; still-open, in-progress and waiting-for-parts plumbing requests have no closing date and are excluded.
Days to close = closing date minus opening date, counted in calendar days, so a request closed the same day counts as 0.
All time periods in the data are included (no date range limited), because none was requested.

cases.question: Leases ending between 2026-10-01 and 2026-12-31.

usage.review_restated: For every lease with an end date from 1 October 2026 through 31 December 2026 inclusive, the SQL lists the lease ID, tenant name, unit number, building name and city, start and end dates, status label, and the unit's monthly rent, sorted by end date, building and unit. It returns 6 rows.

cases.title: Leases ending 1 Oct – 31 Dec 2026
cases.sql:
SELECT l.lease_id AS "Lease ID",
       t.first_name || ' ' || t.last_name AS "Tenant",
       u.unit_number AS "Unit",
       b.name AS "Building",
       b.city AS "City",
       l.start_date AS "Lease Start",
       l.end_date AS "Lease End",
       s.label AS "Lease Status",
       u.monthly_rent AS "Monthly Rent"
FROM lease l
JOIN lease_status s ON s.status_id = l.status_id
JOIN tenant t ON t.tenant_id = l.tenant_id
JOIN unit u ON u.unit_id = l.unit_id
JOIN building b ON b.building_id = u.building_id
WHERE l.end_date >= '2026-10-01' AND l.end_date <= '2026-12-31'
ORDER BY l.end_date, b.name, u.unit_number
assumptions: "Ending between 2026-10-01 and 2026-12-31" means the lease's scheduled end date falls anywhere from 1 October through 31 December 2026, inclusive.
All lease statuses are included (ended, evicted, notice given, etc.) since the question is about end dates, not about current status.
Leases with no recorded end date (about a third of all leases) cannot fall in the window and are excluded.

cases.question: Which buildings have an elevator and more than 10 units?

usage.review_restated: The SQL returns each building whose elevator flag equals 1 and that has more than 10 linked unit rows, showing its name, street, city, build year, and total unit count, sorted by unit count descending.

cases.title: Buildings with an elevator and more than 10 units
cases.sql:
SELECT b.name AS building,
       b.street AS street,
       b.city AS city,
       b.built_year AS built_year,
       COUNT(u.unit_id) AS unit_count
FROM building b
JOIN unit u ON u.building_id = b.building_id
WHERE b.has_elevator = 1
GROUP BY b.building_id, b.name, b.street, b.city, b.built_year
HAVING COUNT(u.unit_id) > 10
ORDER BY unit_count DESC, b.name
assumptions: "Has an elevator" means the building's elevator flag is set to yes.
"More than 10 units" means 11 or more units recorded in the building (counting all units in the system, regardless of occupancy).
Each unit belongs to exactly one building, so units were counted per building without double counting.

cases.question: Evicted tenants and their email addresses.

usage.review_restated: The SQL returns one row per lease whose status label is "Evicted", showing the tenant's full name, email, phone, building name, unit number, and the lease start and end dates, sorted by last and first name.

cases.title: Evicted tenants and their email addresses
cases.sql:
SELECT t.first_name || ' ' || t.last_name AS tenant_name,
       t.email AS email_address,
       t.phone AS phone,
       b.name AS building,
       u.unit_number AS unit_number,
       l.start_date AS lease_start,
       l.end_date AS lease_end
FROM lease l
JOIN lease_status s ON l.status_id = s.status_id
JOIN tenant t ON l.tenant_id = t.tenant_id
LEFT JOIN unit u ON l.unit_id = u.unit_id
LEFT JOIN building b ON u.building_id = b.building_id
WHERE s.label = 'Evicted'
ORDER BY t.last_name, t.first_name
assumptions: "Evicted" means the lease's current status is the stored status value "Evicted" — 16 leases match.
Each tenant has exactly one lease on file, so each evicted tenant appears once (no duplicates).
Included the unit, building and lease dates as context; the email address is the tenant's address on file.
No date range was applied — this covers all evictions on record, whenever they happened.

cases.question: How many plumbin requests are waiting_part?
cases.title: Plumbing requests waiting on parts
cases.sql: SELECT 'plumbing' AS category, 'waiting_parts' AS state, COUNT(*) AS request_count FROM maintenance WHERE category = 'plumbing' AND state = 'waiting_parts'
assumptions: "Waiting_part" was read as the stored status 'waiting_parts' (on hold for spare parts).
Counts are of maintenance requests, all dates included (no date range applied).

cases.question: Show open electricle maintenance requests with their unit.

usage.review_restated: This SQL returns electrical maintenance requests whose state is exactly 'open', each with its request number, date opened, days open as of 21 October 2026, priority, unit number, building name, city, and assigned staff name, sorted by priority and then by oldest first.

cases.title: Open Electrical Maintenance Requests by Unit
cases.sql:
SELECT m.request_id AS request_number,
       m.opened AS date_opened,
       CAST(julianday('2026-10-21') - julianday(m.opened) AS INTEGER) AS days_open,
       m.priority AS priority,
       u.unit_number AS unit,
       b.name AS building,
       b.city AS city,
       (COALESCE(s.first_name,'') || ' ' || COALESCE(s.last_name,'')) AS assigned_to
FROM maintenance m
JOIN unit u ON u.unit_id = m.unit_id
JOIN building b ON b.building_id = u.building_id
LEFT JOIN staff s ON s.staff_id = m.assigned_to
WHERE m.state = 'open'
  AND m.category = 'electrical'
ORDER BY CASE m.priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 WHEN 'normal' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END,
         m.opened
assumptions: "Open" means the request's status is literally Open — requests that are In Progress or Waiting for Parts are excluded.
Electrical covers only requests categorised as Electrical (not plumbing, heating, appliance, pest or general).
"With their unit" is shown as unit number together with the building name and city, because the same unit number exists in multiple buildings.
Days open is counted from the date opened up to today, 21 October 2026.
Results are ordered most urgent first, then oldest first.

Check: Check the meaning of "open": the query keeps only requests whose state is exactly 'open', so electrical requests that are In Progress or Waiting for Parts are silently left out, even though a business user would usually still call them open. If the full set of unfinished requests is wanted, the state filter needs to include those statuses.
